description: Use when ARC inputs compress to smaller output grids.

# ARC compression hypothesis checking

Use for ARC tasks where a regular, periodic, or highly structured input maps to a smaller output. This supplements the general `continual-arc-solving` workflow with a strict evidence gate for compression rules.

## Method

1. Record both input and output dimensions from every demo. A drastic change in shape is itself a key part of the rule; do not assume output size from the visible markers.
2. Identify repeated units, separator bands, and candidate sampling positions. Enumerate possible compression maps (cell, block, intersection, or marker summary) instead of choosing one by visual salience.
3. For each candidate map, compute the full predicted demo output, including default/background values and cells with no apparent marker. Reject a map if even one output cell or dimension differs.
4. Keep selection and encoding separate: establish which source region contributes to each output cell, then establish how its colors/content are encoded.
5. Following incorrect feedback, treat the entire hypothesis as rejected. Re-check mapping, offsets, palette encoding, and output dimensions; do not patch the prior answer by swapping a conspicuous color.
6. Request an additional demo when plausible mappings predict observably different outputs. Otherwise, once a mapping exactly reproduces the demo and yields a concrete test prediction, submit it.
7. Validate output shape and colors before serialization, and retain the action-only JSON protocol.

## Pitfalls

- A marker color visible in the test is not necessarily the output color; the output may encode a different feature or use a global rule.
- Large periodic inputs can contain irregular boundary bands; derive macro dimensions from actual repeated structure, not simply marker count.
- A 1×1 demonstration does not establish that the answer is the first, last, brightest, or most frequent marker. The exact value must be explained by the same rule that maps the demo input to its output.

See `references/failed-compression-submission.md` for a compact post-error checklist and examples of what to re-evaluate.

# Demo request budgeting and complete replay

A demo request is a scored action, not a default follow-up. After every returned pair, extract its full input/output dimensions and determine what feature or lattice maps into each output cell. Check all output values, including default-looking cells, and every relevant source location that did not contribute. Keep candidate mappings explicit: macro-grid dimensions, separator/intersection coordinates, sampling offset, orientation, and any encoding from source colors to output values.

Before requesting another pair, name the live alternatives and the exact observation a new pair could provide that would distinguish them and alter the current test prediction. Do not request pairs consecutively without first analyzing the one just received. The cap is a maximum, not a quota; stop requesting once evidence supports a complete test prediction.

After an incorrect submission, reject the whole candidate, not just its conspicuous color or dimensions. Reconstruct the demo mapping anew and validate the complete candidate against every demo before another submission. Binary feedback does not localize a bad cell or certify parts of the prior guess. Avoid arbitrary tiny-grid variants; only submit a materially different mapping justified by demonstrations.

# Demo-request checkpoint for compressed ARC tasks

After each returned pair, stop and extract its full evidence before requesting more: record the input/output shapes, how each output cell maps to the input, and whether the proposed map explains every cell. Name the remaining competing mappings and what each predicts. Request another pair only if these predictions differ; otherwise apply the best demo-validated map to the test and submit. A streak of requests without incorporating intervening pairs wastes the information already purchased and increases cost. In a task with an apparently featureless test, do not assume the tiny output is a fixed value: use the demonstrations to determine which source structure, including separators or marked intersections, is selected.

# After an incorrect compressed-grid answer

Use this checklist when the evaluator rejects a compressed output. Incorrect feedback rejects the whole prediction, not just its color or one coordinate.

1. Re-read the demo dimensions and output values literally; record them before interpreting the test.
2. Reconstruct the repeated structure and enumerate credible candidate compression/sampling rules.
3. Test every candidate against the complete demonstration, including output shape, blank/default cells, and conspicuous unchanged markers.
4. Separate what source element is selected from how that element becomes an output value.
5. Only submit a rule whose complete prediction matches the demo. If multiple demo-consistent candidates remain, request another example only when they predict different observable outcomes.
6. Do not respond to an incorrect 1×1 guess by trying another salient color without a newly justified mapping.

For recurring periodic layouts, `continual-arc-solving/references/compression-submission-gate.md` has additional lattice-specific checks.

# Re-deriving rejected panel-compression predictions

Use this when a test grid contains aligned panels separated by a divider and an output compresses those panels into a smaller grid, especially after one or more rejected submissions.

1. Parse the panels independently, excluding the divider. Confirm equal dimensions and exact source coordinates for each corresponding output cell.
2. For each demo, compare output support against each panel: panel A foreground, panel B foreground, intersection, union, XOR/difference, and any explicitly evidenced encoding. Compute the candidate output for every coordinate; do not infer from only salient patterns.
3. Use both positive and negative evidence. An output foreground cell must satisfy the proposed rule, while every zero output must be explained too. Identify near-matches where one panel has foreground but the output remains zero; these distinguish intersection from copying or union.
4. Verify color mapping and output dimensions separately from the selection rule. A constant output foreground color does not imply that all colored source cells should be preserved.
5. After a failed submission, freeze the rejected grid as a disproven whole. Do not make a fresh hand-transcribed mask from the same source panel. Reconstruct the panels and generate candidate outputs with code; compare each entire generated grid to the demo before applying the rule to the test.
6. Keep row/column offsets explicit (e.g., right panel begins after the separator), assert each panel/output row width, and serialize only after a final dimensions and palette check.

This workflow is a candidate-generating checklist, not a claim that any particular panel operator applies. A rule is admissible only if it exactly reproduces all available demonstration outputs.

# Large periodic-lattice audit: avoid unsupported compression

A highly regular input with occasional colored values embedded in divider bands can look like a table, but visual regularity alone does not establish the output indexing scheme.

## Evidence-first procedure

1. For each demo, write the exact source row/column coordinates of all horizontal and vertical divider bands and every non-background anomaly. Keep 0-based versus 1-based indexing explicit.
2. Record the output dimensions independently. Do not infer dimensions by counting colored markers, periods, or gaps.
3. Build a proposed source-to-output coordinate map. For each output cell—including the ordinary/background-valued cells—name the source coordinate, source region, or aggregation operation that produces it.
4. Apply that same coordinate map and color rule to every demo and compare every output cell. If any cell or dimension is unexplained, reject the rule or request a distinguishing demo.
5. On the test, construct the full grid from the validated mapping and verify row count, every row width, and legal colors before submission.

## Failure pattern to avoid

In one lattice task, two demonstrations had notably different input/output dimensions and colored marker patterns. A speculative output was submitted without first demonstrating an exact cell-by-cell mapping from both examples; the proposed shape was based on a weak reading of the crossings. Treat this as a failed hypothesis, not evidence for a particular output shape or color rule. When the map remains ambiguous, spend a demo request to distinguish live hypotheses rather than submit an unsupported table.

This complements `periodic-divider-lattices.md`; it does not assert a task-specific transformation.

# Periodic divider-lattice compression

When a large grid is a repeating texture crossed by horizontal and vertical colored bands, interpret it as a compressed table. For every demo:

1. Record separator rows and columns, and calculate both separator counts and the gaps between them. The output may index gaps rather than lines, so a shape of (number of horizontal separators − 1) × (number of vertical separators − 1) is a hypothesis to test, not an automatic rule.
2. Associate each output coordinate with a candidate source compartment. Compare possible representatives (separator intersections, near-corner cells, internal samples, or the compartment's marker) against every output cell, including apparently empty/default cells.
3. Separate coordinate mapping from color extraction. First derive which compartment maps to each output cell; then identify which position/value in that compartment is copied or encoded. Verify offsets and edge compartments.
4. Do this with all demos before requesting another. Consecutive requests without analyzing prior pairs waste budget and obscure whether another example would distinguish live hypotheses.
5. A candidate must reproduce the full demo output and dimensions exactly before applying it to the test. A compression guess based on output shape or a few obvious markers is insufficient.

Pitfall: separator colors and decorative periodic texture can be visually salient but irrelevant. Do not assume output values come from the bands; validate a precise sample map across every pair.

# Post-rejection audit for compressed outputs

Use this after a compressed-grid submission is rejected, especially when the test input is much smaller than the demonstrations.

1. **Stop color/marker tweaking.** The rejection invalidates the full proposed mapping, not just an output cell. Do not submit a cosmetically altered version of the same grid.
2. **Rebuild a dimension table from every demo:** input height × width, separator coordinates, candidate panel dimensions, output height × width. Verify whether the output copies one panel, combines panels, filters rows/columns, or encodes a feature. Equal heights alone do not establish a direct panel copy.
3. **Track source-to-output coordinates explicitly.** For every demo row, compare each candidate source panel against the output cell-by-cell, including zeros. Identify whether output color values are copied, recolored, or indicate a relation between panels. A matching subset of nonzero cells is insufficient.
4. **Treat test shape as evidence, not a license to extrapolate.** A small test and demonstrations with different output widths do not justify guessing an output dimension from visible symbols. Establish the width rule and encoding before constructing a submission.
5. **After two wrong guesses, reset the hypothesis ledger.** List what each rejected output assumed, what observation contradicts each assumption, and what genuinely distinct rule remains. Spend another demo request only if a concrete distinction between candidate rules is expected to clarify the test; otherwise use remaining attempts on evidence-based, materially distinct predictions.

Keep the final interaction action-only: exactly one valid JSON action per turn. This audit is a recovery procedure, not a claim about any particular panel-combination rule.

# Post-rejection recovery for compressed lattice outputs

A wrong full-grid submission validates none of its shape, cells, or extraction rule. Freeze it; do not treat the binary rejection as evidence that only one conspicuous value was wrong.

Before another submission, replay every demonstration from scratch: record exact input/output dimensions, identify the source position or region for each output cell (including ordinary-valued cells), and check the complete output cell by cell. Only transfer a map to the test when it reproduces all demos. Do not infer test dimensions by counting anomalies, crossings, or periods unless the exact relation is demo-validated. If demos leave materially different test predictions, request another pair; otherwise submit the best fully validated rule, not a local cosmetic variant.

# Recovery after repeated incorrect compressed-grid submissions

An evaluator's binary incorrect signal rejects the full proposed grid. It does not certify any cells, coordinates, sampling map, or color rule. Freeze each rejected candidate; do not infer that its broad rule was right except for one conspicuous value.

## Before acting again

1. Replay every demonstration literally: dimensions, all output values (including background/default-looking cells), and repeated source structure.
2. Separate uncertainties: output shape, lattice alignment, sampled location, selector, value encoding, and treatment of empty cells.
3. List materially different rules that each reproduce every known demo, with their concrete test outputs. Reject any rule that fails even one output cell or predicts unobserved changes to unchanged regions.
4. If the live rules predict different test outputs, request a demo only when its possible result can distinguish them. Otherwise submit the best-supported rule.
5. Never submit cosmetic variants of a rejected grid (such as shifting one mark or changing one salient color) without a newly demo-supported mapping. Recheck serialized dimensions and row widths independently.

Keep this checkpoint compact and internal in action-only evaluations; emit exactly the required action JSON.

# Lattice compression: structure first, test-sized output second

In an instance with repeated horizontal and vertical divider bands, do not infer the answer dimensions by counting only marked intersections. Markers can be sparse, absent in entire rows/columns, or concentrated in one panel, while the output can still summarize the complete lattice.

For every demonstration, record the row/column band coordinates and derive the number of macro-cells from the repeated structure, accounting for any partial edge cell. Then make a coordinate table relating each output cell to candidate source coordinates or panel locations. Test a consistent sampling/encoding rule against every output entry, including default-colored entries and marker colors that disappear. Explicitly separate output shape, source-cell selection, and color encoding.

Before requesting another example, first analyze all existing pairs. Name the exact competing mappings and the test cells where their predictions diverge; a new demo is worthwhile only if it can resolve that divergence. Before a second submission after binary rejection, discard the whole previous candidate and verify a materially different complete mapping on every demo—never cycle through guessed tiny grids or isolated color swaps.

# Budgeted ARC demonstration analysis

Use during demonstration-driven ARC tasks when each requested pair consumes score budget. This class-level companion to `continual-arc-solving` focuses on disciplined evidence collection and hypothesis updates.

## Mandatory checkpoint after every pair

1. Compare the new input and output exhaustively. Record dimensions, palette, every changed coordinate with old→new colors, and relevant unchanged lookalikes. Distinguish the rule's **selector** (which seeds/objects/regions are acted on) from the **operation** (fill, extend, recolor, copy), direction, extent, endpoint encoding, and exceptions.
2. Update the hypothesis from all pairs so far. Do not issue several requests sequentially without doing this analysis between them.
3. Before requesting another demo, be able to state all three: (a) the leading hypothesis and its exact prediction on the current test, (b) a materially different alternative that still fits all observed pairs, and (c) an observation from a prospective demo that would distinguish them and could change the answer. If one is absent, analyze more or submit the best-supported rule instead.
4. Treat the demo cap as a limit, not a goal. Requests have a score cost. More data is valuable only when it can resolve an ambiguity relevant to the test prediction; confirmation alone is not automatically worth another request.

## Submission and recovery

- Before submission, validate the proposed rule against every changed cell and every relevant unchanged cell in every demo. Do not infer a broad fill solely from a visually salient boundary or seed.
- For sparse seeds and boundary markers, test independently which seed/alignment selects each ray, its direction and stopping point, endpoint color, and whether boundary runs are themselves transformed. Demos may contain multiple structurally similar but unselected markers; negative evidence is decisive.
- A wrong submission rejects the whole grid, not one coordinate. Reassess selection, operation, range, color, edge cases, and dimensions rather than making a cosmetic adjustment or reusing a guess.
- Preserve action-only interfaces: the puzzle response must end with exactly one valid action JSON object and no explanatory prose.

## References

See `continual-arc-solving` for general ARC parsing and output validation, and `arc-hypothesis-ledger` for coordinate bookkeeping and binary-feedback recovery.

# Action checkpoint after each demo

A returned example must trigger analysis, not an automatic request for another example. Before taking the next action:

1. Compare input/output dimensions and output content with every prior pair.
2. State a candidate transformation and calculate what it predicts for the current test.
3. If considering another demo, name a materially different rule that still fits all known pairs and a specific observation in a future pair that would separate the two and could change the test prediction.
4. If no such discriminating observation exists, do not spend a demo for reassurance; analyze further or submit the best-supported prediction.

The score cost and action-only reply format do not remove this analysis requirement. Emit exactly one protocol-valid action only after the checkpoint is complete.

# Cross-demo analysis before spending another request

In multi-demo tasks, a request is a scored action, so do not treat a new pair as an automatic prompt to request the next one. After each pair:

1. Compare its input and output exactly, recording every changed coordinate/color and relevant unchanged lookalikes.
2. Reconcile it with every earlier pair, checking whether dimensions, orientation, palette, selected row/column, or completeness of a marked run vary. Separate selector, operation, endpoint/extent, and endpoint color.
3. Write down the leading rule and its exact predicted test output, plus a materially different rule that fits all examples and its distinct test prediction.
4. Request another pair only if a concrete possible observation in that pair would distinguish these alternatives and could change the test answer enough to justify the cost. Otherwise submit the strongest supported prediction rather than spending a request on vague uncertainty or confirmation.

Keep the response action-only when required. Never emit prose alongside the one JSON action.

# Cross-divider panels: compare patterns in local coordinates

Use this note when demos show an otherwise empty grid split by one full horizontal and one full vertical divider, with newly colored cells appearing in the resulting panels.

## Analysis procedure

1. Record the divider row and column; treat them as preserved structure unless a demo proves otherwise.
2. Separate the four panels and convert each changed cell to panel-local `(row, column)` coordinates. Compare each panel independently across examples, even when panel dimensions differ.
3. Tabulate the exact selected cells, including zeros that stayed zero. Check whether selection is periodic, edge-relative, shape-based, or differs by panel; do not force one global checkerboard, symmetric fill, or identical panel mask to fit only part of the evidence.
4. Use both demos to validate a single explicit selector and operation. The first example in this session showed panel outputs with distinct, selective 0→4 patterns; the second showed different local motifs and panel asymmetries. The apparent crossed grid alone did not establish a checkerboard rule.
5. On a rejected output, treat the entire candidate as unvalidated. Re-derive selection from demo coordinates rather than submitting a cosmetic variant of the same broad pattern.

## Pitfall

A tempting but unsupported approach is to use parity-based alternation throughout every quadrant. It can look orderly and still miss panel-specific structure. Before submission, reproduce every demo output exactly—including untouched zeros—and only then apply the rule to a new grid.

This is a general analysis caution, not a solved rule for any particular task: the exact selector must come from the demos.

# Decide after every returned demo

A demo response is a decision point, not an automatic cue to request the next pair. Before any further action:

1. Compare input/output dimensions and determine whether the input is preserved, embedded, tiled, or expanded; account for every output region, not just the apparent added area.
2. Test the candidate operation against the entire output and compare it with all prior pairs. Separate an explainable transformation from cells or regions that merely look random.
3. State the current best rule and its concrete prediction on the test, plus a materially different alternative that still fits the evidence.
4. Request another demo only if you can name a specific observation that would distinguish those rules and could change the test answer enough to justify the cost. Otherwise analyze further or submit the best-supported prediction.

Avoid reflexive consecutive demo requests. The existence of a demo cap does not imply that more examples are useful, especially when the observed outputs do not support a coherent transformation.

# Exact stencil placements in noisy grids

Use this when a demo shows a small colored seed that appears to recur as a set of edits within a noisy binary field.

1. Capture the seed's non-background cells as offsets from its bounding-box origin. Preserve holes and spacing; do not reduce it to an approximate shape.
2. Enumerate only translations initially. Consider rotations/reflections only if an example explicitly supports them.
3. For every candidate origin, test every stencil offset against the input and check the whole output for edits that candidate predicts but demos do not make. A partial match is not evidence for a placement.
4. Infer collision rules (all cells must be background, overlap prohibited, etc.) from positive and negative examples. Confirm whether the seed is preserved and whether copied cells take the seed color.
5. Apply the validated placements only; preserve all unrelated cells. Check dimensions and serialize the full output carefully.

A useful verification pattern is to compare the candidate-generated edit-coordinate set against the exact input/output difference set, rather than relying on visual inspection.

# Paired-object placement cues

When a demo contains two distinct objects (often different colors), and the output preserves or transforms one while removing the other, do not treat the disappearing object as irrelevant by default. Compare its exact cell offsets and bounding box to the output's generated geometry. It may encode the target placement, selector, orientation, or extent rather than serve as a disposable distractor.

Workflow:
1. Inventory both shapes as coordinate-offset sets relative to their bounding-box origins.
2. Align each candidate marker against the output changes and see whether the mapping is exact, including holes and unequal dimensions.
3. Test reflection/copy rules and marker-as-anchor rules against every unchanged region in all demos.
4. On a rejected test prediction, reassess the role of both objects and the operation class; do not merely shift or tweak the previous output.
5. Request a further demo only when a specific configuration can distinguish the competing marker roles and would alter the predicted output.

This lesson was prompted by demos where a lower color-6 marker disappeared while color-4 content appeared to reflect vertically; the reflection-only prediction on the test was incorrect. Treat that as evidence to revisit marker placement/selection, not as proof of a particular alternative transformation.

# Paired-object reflection cues: analysis checklist

When demos show one colored pattern being expanded and a separate colored object disappearing, treat the relation as an unresolved **selector + operation** problem, not as proof that the disappearing object is simply an occlusion mask.

For each pair:
1. Record the complete coordinates of the persistent-color object, disappearing-color object, and all newly added cells.
2. Test candidate symmetry axes and reflection directions by comparing the seed's exact cell offsets with the additions. Distinguish horizontal reflection, vertical reflection, rotations, and copying; account for every added cell and every absent expected cell.
3. Record the cue's orientation and relative position to the pattern separately. Across demos, test whether the cue selects direction, axis, or merely identifies the target. Do not infer one fixed axis from a single example.
4. Apply the resulting mapping to the test only if the cue-to-transform rule is consistent across all demos. Keep the cue-removal behavior distinct from the pattern completion rule.
5. After an incorrect submission, reject the whole candidate. Reconstruct its exact predicted change set, identify which untested assumptions it bundled (target, axis, direction, extent, cue handling), and choose a materially different evidence-supported candidate or request a demo that distinguishes the remaining alternatives.

This checklist is motivated by pairs where a 4-pattern is extended while a separate 6-pattern vanishes. Apparent reflection completion is plausible, but axis and direction must be inferred from the full cross-demo relation rather than guessed from the test layout.

# Mandatory analysis after each demo

A new turn that includes a demonstration is a checkpoint, not a cue to reflexively ask for another pair. First compare the input and output exactly, record changed coordinates and colors, distinguish selector from operation/extent, and update the rule's prediction on the current test. Then decide whether the accumulated examples already determine an actionable answer.

Request another demo only when you can state (1) the leading rule and its concrete test prediction, (2) a materially distinct alternative fitting all known pairs, and (3) a specific observation in a prospective demo that would distinguish them and could change the prediction. If those are not clear, continue analyzing or submit the best-supported rule; do not spend requests without a discriminator. This is especially important when examples look heterogeneous: compare their shared transformation rather than treating each as unrelated pattern noise.

In strict action-only tasks, perform the analysis internally and emit exactly one action JSON. A repeated sequence of demo requests without integrating the evidence burns budget and can end with the instance unsolved.

# Symmetry and occlusion reconstruction from demo diffs

Use when one grid contains prominent blocks of a placeholder color embedded in an otherwise highly structured pattern, while demos show those blocks removed/replaced in the output.

## Evidence procedure

1. Record every changed coordinate and its input/output color; separately record candidate placeholder-mask cells and untouched patterned regions.
2. Treat the mask as a selector/occluder hypothesis, not as an output color rule. Compare the mask's coordinates with plausible counterpart positions under rotation, reflection, or repeated tiling.
3. For each demo, check whether the output at mask positions matches the unmasked counterpart from the input. Confirm mapping across all changed and unchanged positions; account for asymmetry and offsets.
4. Apply only the established mapping to test-mask cells. If both a cell and its proposed counterpart are masked, the demos may not determine that value; seek another mapping or evidence rather than filling by intuition.
5. Once multiple demos vary the mask placement but consistently reveal the same patterned source, update the test prediction and stop requesting confirmation demos unless a live ambiguity remains.

## Lesson from this session

The three observed input/output pairs each replace irregular 2-colored placeholder patches with values matching counterpart positions in a patterned background, suggesting that the patch positions are occlusions in a symmetry/repetition transform. The test also has a large central placeholder patch; it should trigger explicit symmetry/repetition analysis before asking for another pair. This is a diagnostic lead, not proof of a specific transform: establish the coordinate map against every demo before submitting.

# ARC enclosure transformations

Use for ARC tasks where closed outlines, frames, or loops contain interior cells that are transformed.

## Workflow

1. Inventory every candidate outline on the entire grid, noting boundary color, bounding box, interior dimensions, shape, and whether the interior is uniformly background.
2. Compare demo input/output cell by cell. Separate unchanged outline from changed interior; record every enclosure that changed and every plausible enclosure that did not.
3. Infer selection and encoding separately: determine which outline qualifies, then determine how its interior geometry or contents map to output colors/patterns. Measure interior only (exclude border cells).
4. Test the rule against every relevant enclosure in every demo, including negative evidence. Do not infer an odd/even or size-to-color rule from one example alone.
5. Apply the demonstrated rule consistently to all matching enclosures across the test grid, including distant, lower, and right-side objects. Preserve borders and all non-enclosed background.
6. Audit the changed-cell set against the full grid inventory for missed matches, accidental fills of open cavities, coordinate mistakes, dimensions, and valid palette values.

## Pitfalls

- An interior can look enclosed but be open through a gap; verify the actual boundary connectivity.
- Do not limit transformation to the visually prominent cluster. Remote matching frames are easy to miss when transcribing a large grid.
- Color mapping may depend on interior size or shape, but only use distinctions demonstrated by evidence.
- A single incorrect submission rejects the full grid, so after feedback re-evaluate the rule and whole-grid application rather than tweaking one conspicuous cell.

For a compact size/color recording and full-grid changed-cell audit, see `references/whole-grid-enclosure-audit.md`.

# Negative-space connectivity analysis

Some ARC transformations target background-color pockets enclosed by foreground barriers rather than interiors of tidy rectangular outlines. Detect these globally and objectively:

1. For each plausible background color, flood-fill its cells from every grid-edge cell using 4-neighbor adjacency.
2. Any cells of that color not reached from the border belong to enclosed components. Record each component's coordinates, size, bounding box, and neighboring foreground colors.
3. Compare the resulting component map cell-by-cell with demonstration edits. Include unchanged cavities as negative evidence; connectivity alone may identify candidates, while another feature determines selection.
4. Infer target selection separately from the operation/color mapping. In a test grid, transform only components supported by the demos, preserving the boundary and all border-connected background.
5. When an initial visual guess is rejected, reconsider global topology instead of making a nearby line/column adjustment. Irregular arrangements of barriers may create closed pockets that are easy to miss by eye.

Use orthogonal connectivity unless examples demonstrate diagonal connectivity. Before submission, audit exact changed coordinates and ensure no border-connected background was accidentally included.

# Whole-grid enclosure audit

Use this worksheet when a task transforms cavities inside outlines.

| Object | Bounding box | Interior size/shape | Closed boundary? | Input interior | Changed cells/output color | Candidate rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

For each demo, enumerate all visually plausible enclosures and record both changed and unchanged cases. Count interior dimensions strictly between border rows/columns. Determine whether the rule selects by closure, size, shape, fill state, or another feature; keep selection separate from color encoding. In the test, enumerate every candidate across the full grid, apply only the evidence-supported rule, and verify that the complete changed-cell set is accounted for without touching borders or open background.

# ARC hypothesis ledger and recovery

Use when an ARC task has returned only binary correct/incorrect feedback, especially when several plausible output lines, fills, or recolorings exist.

## Recovery sequence

1. **Freeze the rejected candidate.** A wrong whole-grid submission validates none of its cells. Do not infer that the rule was right except for one guessed coordinate or extent.
2. **Reconstruct the evidence.** For every demo, inventory each changed cell as `(row, column, old color → new color)`. Note conspicuous unchanged objects and regions. Separate target selection from operation and boundary/extent rules.
3. **Keep a hypothesis ledger.** For each materially distinct candidate, write its concise rule, how it reproduces every demo (positive and negative evidence), and its precise test-grid prediction. Mark rejected hypotheses and the evidence rejecting them. Do not retry nearby columns/rows or tweak line extents without a new, demo-grounded reason.
4. **Request targeted evidence only when useful.** Name the unresolved alternatives and the observation in a possible new demo that would distinguish them. Request another pair only if the result could change the test prediction enough to justify its score cost; otherwise submit the best-supported rule.
5. **Build and audit the output.** Use a consistent coordinate convention (prefer zero-based internally), record dimensions and divider coordinates, apply only edits explained by the rule, and inspect every changed coordinate. Verify the complete output against every demo before serializing.
6. **Respect action-only protocols.** In constrained ARC conversations, do all analysis internally and end with exactly one valid action JSON object. No explanatory prose should accompany puzzle actions.

## Pitfalls

- An incorrect grid does not localize the error: selector, transformation, extent, collision handling, dimensions, or coordinate transcription may be wrong.
- Repeated shifts of a full-height stripe are not distinct hypotheses unless evidence identifies the shift.
- A rule can fit all positive demo edits yet fail because it also predicts changes in an unchanged region.
- Re-reading a demo informally can cause index drift. List exact coordinates and separately verify one-based puzzle notation against zero-based arrays.

# Divider stripes versus transformation targets

When a grid has a full-height colored stripe near a patterned region, do not infer that the stripe is to be recolored just because a demonstration shows a same-colored replacement stripe elsewhere. Establish the stripe's role from exact cellwise demo differences:

1. Record all changed cells and their original colors/coordinates. Identify whether the change covers a full column, a segment, or only an object's footprint.
2. Separate three candidate mechanisms: fixed divider/separator; positional cue or destination marker; direct recoloring target. Test each against unchanged areas and the test layout.
3. If feedback rejects a global stripe recoloring, discard that entire interpretation. Do not submit another column chosen by a nearby visual alignment; determine a materially different operation from demo evidence.
4. For a local object, check whether its shape, holes, or protrusions encode an instruction independent of the full-height stripe. Avoid transforming background rows unless the demonstration establishes that extent.

A single example can underdetermine the stripe's semantic role. Pay for another demo only when you can name an observation that distinguishes candidates and would change the test prediction; otherwise submit the best evidence-backed alternative.

# No-repeat rule after a rejected ARC submission

When evaluator feedback is only binary, it does not validate any individual cell, subrule, or coordinate in the submitted grid. Record the rejected candidate as wholly unverified. Do not submit the identical grid again: absent new evidence, it has the same unsupported prediction and only adds another wrong-submission cost.

Before using another submission, derive a materially different candidate from the demonstrations, and verify the complete prediction against every known input/output pair, including unchanged cells. If the examples leave a genuine ambiguity and a new pair could change the test prediction, request that targeted demo instead of repeating the rejected candidate. For strict action-only tasks, all comparison is internal and the response remains one action JSON only.

This supplements the recovery sequence in the parent skill; it does not recommend speculative edits to a previously rejected grid.

# Rejected-grid deduplication audit

Before each ARC submission after binary feedback, record the prior candidate (full grid or a concise change mask/rule signature) and compare the new candidate against it. A repeat of the same grid is never a meaningful experiment: binary feedback gives no cell-level confirmation. A lightly edited grid that preserves the same unsupported selector or transformation is also not a new hypothesis. Stop and return to the demonstrations: re-evaluate object selection, mapping, encoding, extent, untouched regions, and dimensions; derive a distinct prediction and verify it against all demos before submitting. With no demos remaining, spend each remaining attempt only on a substantially revised, demo-grounded hypothesis. Keep the user's action-only protocol unchanged.

# Recovery gate after repeated rejection

Use this when a task has had at least two incorrect whole-grid submissions and there are still demo requests available.

1. Freeze the rejected grids; binary feedback does not identify which cells or assumptions were wrong. Never resubmit one verbatim.
2. Reconstruct the demos cell-by-cell, including unchanged lookalikes. Separate selector, operation, direction, extent, color, and collision/endpoint behavior.
3. Record each rejected candidate and the assumption it depended on. A retry must be a materially revised rule supported by evidence, not a nearby coordinate, extent, or color variant.
4. Before spending another demo, state what unresolved, materially different rules remain, how their test predictions differ, and what possible observation in a new pair would discriminate them. Request only if that evidence could change the answer.
5. Before submitting, check all dimensions and row lengths, preserve untargeted cells, and ensure the serialized grid reflects the revised rule. Audit the candidate against every demo, including unchanged regions.
6. Keep any required interaction action-only; all analysis stays internal and the response contains only the protocol-valid JSON action.

Common trap: repeated guesses at line completions can look like progress while retaining the same unsupported selector/operation hypothesis. After multiple failures, restart from the demos and reconsider the transformation class.

# Continual ARC puzzle solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks where each instance provides a test grid, optional demonstrations, and a constrained action protocol.

## Operating protocol

1. **Honor the interface exactly.** Each puzzle turn requires exactly one action. Finish the response with one valid JSON action object (`submit`, `request_demos`, or, only after the instance is over, `finish`). Do not include commentary or unrelated tool calls when the interface requests only an action.
2. **Parse before inferring.** Record grid dimensions, palette, all non-background cells, and connected components. Check row/column indexing carefully; verify the submitted grid has the required dimensions and only integer colors 0–9.
3. **Use demonstrations as evidence.** Compare each input/output pair cell by cell. Separate preserved background from changed cells; identify whether the change is a recoloring, geometric completion, replication, movement, or global pattern. Locate the seed object and test candidate rules against all changed cells and all unchanged cells, not just a visually compelling subset.
4. **Request another demo when it is more valuable than a guess.** If multiple plausible rules fit the observed example or a candidate rule cannot explain the output comprehensively, request a demo rather than submitting an unsupported transformation. Factor the stated request cost into the decision, but do not treat an unverified guess as established.
5. **Construct output conservatively.** Preserve every cell unless the inferred rule explains its modification. Apply the transformation programmatically or with a carefully checked coordinate map for large grids; inspect the final result for accidental changes, dimensions, and valid colors before submission.
6. **Learn from feedback.** A correct/incorrect signal alone does not identify which cells or rule were wrong. On incorrect feedback, revise or gather further evidence rather than repeating the same candidate.

## Common pitfalls

- Do not conflate “cells matching a visual pattern” with the actual rule unless the demo output confirms the relevant color, direction, overlap, and boundary behavior.
- Do not overwrite background or existing objects as a side effect of a broad pattern-fill operation; explicitly check collisions and exceptions.
- Do not submit a guessed grid merely because a simple geometric predicate can be found in the test. Validate that predicate against the demo output first.
- Do not make extraneous tool calls in an action-only interaction; they add noise and do not improve the puzzle inference.

## Verification checklist

Before a submission, confirm: (a) inferred rule reproduces the demonstration output exactly, (b) all original cells not targeted by that rule remain intact, (c) output dimensions equal the requested dimensions, and (d) the final line is the single required JSON action.

See `references/demo-analysis-checklist.md` for a compact comparison worksheet.

# Evidence checkpoints for ARC compression

See `two-error-recovery.md` for the required process after consecutive wrong submissions in lattice-compression puzzles.

# Staying within the action-only decision budget

In evaluation streams where each turn accepts exactly one JSON action, keep the tool path lean. Load the umbrella skill and only the specific reference needed for the decision. Repeated reads of unchanged references do not supply new puzzle evidence and can consume the available response/time budget before an action is emitted.

After a wrong answer, use the next turn to diagnose from the given feedback and existing demonstrations: list exact changes in the demos, assess which rule assumption failed, and choose between one information-bearing demo request or a materially revised prediction. Do not use repeated reference lookups as a substitute for that analysis.

When feedback says the grid is invalid, first audit serialization: exact row count, exact width for each row, legal integer colors, nested-list format, and a single action JSON. This is distinct from the puzzle rule being incorrect. For long grids, manually re-check each row after editing, including the final cell and row boundaries.

# Action-only ARC interaction discipline

In evaluation protocols that require exactly one JSON action per turn:

- Keep each turn to the puzzle decision and required action. Do not make no-op shell calls or reread unchanged references after the relevant skill guidance has already been loaded; such calls add latency and risk violating the tight interface without supplying puzzle evidence.
- Request a demonstration only when it can resolve a specific ambiguity. When a demo arrives, compare its input and output and incorporate that evidence before deciding whether another request is useful.
- Once the demonstrations support a concrete rule and test prediction, stop requesting examples and submit the constructed grid. Preserve the entire grid except for cells the rule selects, and ensure the final response is exactly the one action object expected by the protocol.

# After an incorrect grid submission

Use this when the evaluator reports only correct/incorrect and gives no cell-level diagnostics.

1. Treat the entire candidate transformation as rejected. Do not resubmit the same grid, or an equivalent candidate with only a superficial difference.
2. Re-derive from the demo: enumerate changed and unchanged cells, test color, orientation, boundaries, offsets, and output dimensions. Negative evidence matters: explain why visually similar cells remained untouched.
3. Separate uncertainty into candidate rules and compare their concrete predictions. Request a demonstration only when you can name an observation that distinguishes them and that observation materially affects the answer.
4. If there are no more useful demonstrations, spend remaining submissions on genuinely distinct hypotheses backed by the grid, rather than repeatedly patching an unsupported guess.
5. For divider-separated patterns, map all regions and determine the divider's role from the full demo. Do not infer a half-plane fill or select a region only because it is visually salient.
6. Validate the output shape using the demonstrated input/output dimension mapping. A plausible cell pattern is not enough if output dimensions were assumed rather than derived.

# Analyze before requesting another demonstration

A demo request is a scored action, not a default follow-up. After each returned pair, first compare input and output exactly: enumerate changed coordinates with old/new colors, identify the transformation, and note salient matching candidates that remained unchanged. Update and test the rule against the entire pair, including negative evidence.

Before another request, state internally the unresolved ambiguity, the competing hypotheses, and the concrete observation a new pair could produce that would distinguish them. If you cannot name such a discriminator, do not request. If the evidence already yields a concrete test prediction, submit rather than continuing to gather examples. Never issue consecutive demo requests without analyzing the pair just received.

In action-only puzzle conversations, do this analysis internally and output only the one required JSON action. Keep the demo-request cost in the decision; a request is worthwhile only when its expected information can resolve uncertainty that materially changes the answer.

# Inferring anchor offsets in template-copy tasks

A common ARC pattern is a fixed, possibly sparse colored template plus isolated markers. A recurring failure mode is to copy the pattern while assuming the marker is centered or aligned to the template's unusual singleton cell.

## Procedure

1. Record the template's complete bounding box and every non-background coordinate relative to its top-left; retain holes and sparse background cells.
2. For each demo marker, compare the source template to the entire output. Identify which placement explains the copied cells, then measure the exact displacement from marker coordinate to template origin (or to a distinctive template coordinate).
3. Check every changed cell and salient unchanged cell. Verify whether the marker itself is part of the copied output, overwritten by a template cell, or preserved; do not infer marker behavior from one placement if another demonstration can resolve it.
4. Test the same anchor offset across all examples, including edge placements and overlapping candidate footprints. A plausible visual alignment is insufficient unless it reproduces each demo exactly.
5. Apply the inferred offset by coordinate arithmetic in a grid copy. Keep source and output distinct, bounds-check every coordinate, and validate dimensions and full diff before submitting.
6. After an incorrect submission, reconsider anchor coordinate, source-cell set, selector, and marker handling as separate hypotheses. Avoid repeated guesses that only shift an otherwise identical copy by one cell.

This complements `references/pattern-copy-validation.md`, which covers exact masks and transformed placements.

# Preventing unanalysed consecutive demo requests

A demonstration request is a scored action, not a neutral pause. After every returned pair, perform a complete input/output comparison before choosing the next action:

1. Record every changed coordinate and its old/new colors; group changes by object or region.
2. Note conspicuous candidate structures and cells that remained unchanged. Use these negatives to constrain the selector, not just the positive changed cells.
3. State the leading rule and its exact prediction for the current test. Keep target selection, operation, output color, extent/boundaries, and collision behavior distinct.
4. Name a materially different alternative that still explains all demos. Request another pair only if a concrete possible observation would distinguish the alternatives and could change the test answer enough to justify the cost.
5. Otherwise submit the best evidence-supported prediction. A demo cap is a maximum, never a target; repeating `request_demos` without integrating the last pair spends budget without increasing confidence.

After an incorrect submission, freeze the entire candidate as unvalidated. Do not make a nearby variant based on binary feedback alone; reassess the rule against all positive and negative demo evidence first.

# Binary feedback and hypothesis revision

When the evaluator only reports correct/incorrect, a failed submission rejects the entire predicted output. It does not validate any cell, subrule, output dimension, or boundary decision.

## Recovery procedure

1. Reconstruct the exact demonstrated edits and conspicuous non-edits. Verify the candidate against the full demo, not only a salient subset.
2. Separate the target selector from the transformation. Check whether the error could be in object choice, fill/recolor operation, boundaries, collision handling, coordinates, or output shape.
3. List genuinely different rules still consistent with the demonstration. For each, derive its distinct prediction on the test and identify cells/regions where those predictions disagree.
4. If another demonstration could choose between those rules, request it rather than spending another speculative submission. If not, submit only a materially revised, demo-consistent hypothesis.
5. After multiple failures, stop making minor variants (for example, changing a length threshold or fill extent) unless new evidence motivates that exact change. Reconsider whether the initial rule family was wrong.
6. Preserve strict action-only output: use any available computation internally, but the reply must end with exactly one valid protocol action.

A simple visual rule inferred from a single example remains a hypothesis even if it fits every changed cell; unchanged examples and alternative selectors matter equally.

# Binary-feedback recovery: never repeat a rejected grid

When a submission is marked incorrect, the signal rejects the entire output and does not localize the cause. Freeze the full candidate rather than treating it as a nearly-correct answer.

1. Record the exact rejected grid or a compact representation of its changed cells so a later attempt cannot accidentally duplicate it.
2. Revisit every demo and enumerate changed as well as unchanged cells. Reassess the selector, transformation, spatial extent, colors, object boundaries, and preservation of background separately.
3. Compare the rejected prediction to the rule it embodied. A new candidate must be materially different and supported by a demo-level explanation; shifting a boundary, changing an arbitrary fill color, or making a cosmetic variant is not evidence-based recovery.
4. If another demonstration is available, request it only when a concrete observation can distinguish plausible rules and affect the test prediction. Analyze each returned pair before deciding whether to ask again.
5. If demos are exhausted, use the strongest distinct hypothesis that accounts for all examples, including negative evidence. Audit dimensions and serialization; do not resubmit a rejected grid.

Maintain the action-only protocol: final response contains exactly one valid action JSON and no explanation.

# Verifying changed-dimension grid mappings

Use when a demonstration output has dimensions that are multiples of its input, or otherwise appears tiled, expanded, reflected, or repeated.

1. Compute the exact output-to-input size ratios, but do not treat the ratios as proof of the transformation.
2. If dimensions permit it, partition the output into source-sized blocks. Compare each block to the input under explicit candidate transforms (identity, horizontal/vertical reflection, rotations, translation/cropping where relevant). Inspect complete rows and columns, not only distinctive colors.
3. Check repeated bands and their order. Repetition could be horizontal/vertical, a reflection pattern, a transformed motif, or a different operation; test candidates against every output cell.
4. Apply a candidate to a new input only after it reproduces the entire demonstration output exactly. If no candidate fits, retain uncertainty and use a demo request only when a concrete alternative prediction would distinguish the hypotheses.
5. A failed submission rejects the full output hypothesis, including its dimensions and coordinate map. Do not make near-identical guesses; reconstruct and verify from the demo evidence first.

This checklist supplements `compressed-grid-error-recovery.md` for cases where the output is enlarged/repeated rather than a lattice compressed to a smaller grid.

# Collinear marker bridging: evidence checklist

Use this when a sparse grid contains same-colored marker cells and demos show some intervening cells recolored.

1. Record all marker coordinates and every changed cell exactly; distinguish marker endpoints from newly colored cells.
2. For each row and column, sort marker coordinates and inspect each interval between consecutive markers. Test whether the intervening cells are filled, partially filled, or left unchanged. Also check whether the rule acts only on adjacent markers or bridges the entire interval between consecutive endpoints.
3. Verify both orientations independently. A rule may connect horizontally and vertically, but should not be generalized to diagonals, hull interiors, or arbitrary shapes without explicit demo evidence.
4. Check endpoints, intersections, overlaps, existing non-background cells, and cells beyond the outermost markers. Reproduce every changed and unchanged demo cell exactly before extrapolating.
5. Generate the candidate prediction for the test input, then check dimensions, palette, and JSON serialization. One attractive alignment is not enough: an over-broad hull or fill can alter large unsupported areas.

Keep this as a candidate family, not a default rule; infer which aligned links are selected from the demonstrations.

# Compressed-output checkpoint lessons

This reference captures a recurring failure mode in large periodic-grid tasks whose outputs are much smaller than their inputs.

## Before each demo request

- Analyze the newly returned pair first. Record input and output dimensions and inspect the entire output against candidate source subgrids/crops and periodic maps.
- State the current best rule, the exact prediction it makes for the test, one alternative that still fits known demos, and what feature in another demo would distinguish them. If no such discriminating evidence exists, another request is probably confirmation rather than useful evidence.
- Do not spend multiple demo requests consecutively without updating this comparison after each returned pair.

## Mapping and submission checkpoint

- Treat output dimension, source-region selection, coordinate offset, and cell-value encoding as separate unknowns.
- Compare candidate coordinate maps against every output cell in every demo; a plausible-looking central pattern or prominent marker is not enough.
- After a wrong submission, discard the complete proposed mapping. Do not try nearby crops, different output sizes, or color swaps unless the alternative is a materially new rule that explains all demos and predicts the test.
- When no exact demo-validated mapping is available, avoid a succession of guesses that differ only cosmetically. Maintain a ledger of rejected candidates and what each error cannot localize.

## Takeaway

Large structured inputs can hide a compact output-selection rule that is not simply “copy the obvious periodic block.” Establish the exact mapping from demonstration evidence before serialization; verify output height, width, and every value.

# Recovering after failed periodic-grid predictions

Use this when a large regular lattice compresses to a small output and a candidate submission is rejected.

- Treat a tiny guessed output or a few salient colors as an unsupported hypothesis; binary feedback rejects the whole answer and does not validate any component.
- Reconstruct the demo mapping from the complete periodic structure: count bands/intersections, establish the macro-grid shape, then map the same within-unit coordinate(s) to each output cell.
- Check every demo output cell, not just distinctive markers. Use differing marker colors and absent/blank positions to test candidate sampling offsets and row/column orientation.
- After an error, change the inferred mapping only when evidence warrants it; do not cycle through arbitrary short grids or color variants. If there are competing mappings, spend a demo request only when it can distinguish them.
- Before submission, verify exact output height and width from the discovered macro-grid and serialize the complete derived grid in the required action object.

## Infer the compression map, not just the output motif

For repeated lattice inputs summarized to a small grid, separately derive (1) output height/width, (2) source coordinate/intersection for each output cell, and (3) the value encoding. Repeated separators or marker groups may define different axes and may be asymmetric. Compare every output cell—including blank/default values—and multiple demos with changed marker placements. One salient marker alignment is not enough to validate the map.

## Use binary feedback without random variants

An incorrect submission rejects the entire candidate. It does not establish that the dimensions, selected region, alignment, or encoding were otherwise right. After an error, list the competing mappings and their concrete predictions, check each against every demo, and request another example only if it could discriminate a specific unresolved choice. Avoid variants that merely alter one color/cell or crop/output dimension without a demo-supported rule change.

## Demo-cost checkpoint

Before each request, state the leading rule and alternative, their different test predictions, and the observation that would distinguish them. Analyze the just-returned pair first; the demo cap is a maximum, not a target. Submit once a complete mapping reproduces all examples and produces a concrete test answer.

Several tempting compressed grids based on apparent repeated horizontal/vertical dividers and marker colors failed even after variants in size and contents. The durable lesson is not a specific mapping: periodic visual structure alone does not identify the correct compression map. Validate a complete coordinate/value map against all output entries before spending submissions.

# Submission gate after a failed periodic-grid prediction

Use when a regular lattice must be summarized into a small output, especially after one or more incorrect guesses.

1. Treat an incorrect result as rejecting the complete output hypothesis; it does not validate any cells, colors, output dimensions, or sampling offset.
2. Before another submission, reconstruct the lattice explicitly: list separator/band coordinates, count the repeated units, and derive the macro-grid dimensions independently of the colorful marker positions.
3. Enumerate candidate sampling maps (for example, which intersection or within-cell coordinate encodes each output cell) and compare each candidate against every output cell in the demonstration, including blank/default values and marker colors. Record candidate mappings and exact contradictions; do not infer the map from just the salient colors.
4. Only submit a test grid after one mapping reproduces the whole demo and yields its complete test output. If two mappings remain plausible, request a demonstration only when a possible result would distinguish them.
5. Avoid a sequence of guessed output sizes, cropped subsets, or selective color variants. Those are not meaningful hypothesis revisions unless supported by a changed, demo-validated mapping.

Check output height and width against the inferred macro-grid before serialization; retain the strict one-action JSON protocol.

In action-only continual-ARC sessions, do not treat `request_demos` as a default follow-up. Once a demo arrives, compare its input and output before selecting the next action: enumerate changed coordinates and color transitions, test candidate transformation families against both changed cells and counterexamples, and record the remaining ambiguity. Request another demo only when a specific plausible outcome would discriminate between the live hypotheses. If the evidence already yields a concrete test prediction, submit it; every extra request incurs cost and repeated unanalysed requests waste the information already supplied.

# Demo and retry discipline in costly ARC streams

This session exposed a costly failure mode: the solver requested several demonstrations in sequence without extracting usable evidence, then submitted an identical candidate repeatedly after binary incorrect feedback. Apply the following class-level safeguards.

## After every demo

- Compare the entire input and output; list exact edits and unchanged lookalikes.
- Update the rule, separating target selection from the operation and extent.
- Do not make another demo request until the latest pair is analyzed.
- Before requesting, name at least two hypotheses still consistent with all evidence, their distinct predictions on the current test, and an observable outcome from a new pair that would distinguish them. If no concrete discriminator exists, stop requesting and submit the best-supported prediction.

## After an incorrect submission

- Binary feedback rejects the whole grid, not one cell. Freeze that candidate; infer nothing about which parts were right.
- Never resubmit the same grid. Avoid superficial variants (one-cell shifts, guessed line lengths, recoloring a conspicuous marker) unless a new demo directly supports that change.
- Revisit the complete evidence and audit selector, transformation, direction, extent, anchor, collisions, and preserved cells. The next submission must be materially distinct and grounded in all demos, including negative evidence.

# Cross-demo evidence checkpoint and request discipline

Use this after each received demo, especially when examples look unrelated or when the request cap is tempting.

1. Compare that pair exactly: record every changed coordinate and old→new color, and note visually plausible unchanged candidates.
2. Compare the transformation across **all** received pairs at the rule level. Demos can vary in palette, dimensions, and geometry while expressing a common relation; avoid treating each pair as isolated or overfitting surface appearance.

If no concrete discriminator exists, submit the best-supported prediction rather than spending the request cost.
5. Never request reflexively or back-to-back without analyzing the latest pair. Demo cap is a ceiling, not a quota.
6. After an incorrect submission, treat the entire candidate as unverified. Re-evaluate the rule against every demo; do not tweak isolated cells or dimensions without new evidence.

# Cross-demo invariant analysis

When a task supplies multiple demonstrations with different sizes, palettes, or layouts, compare the transformation at the rule level rather than matching their raw appearance. For each pair, record exact edits and unchanged candidate objects; separate the invariant selector and operation from variable colors, locations, orientations, and boundary positions.

Before spending another demo request, form the leading rule's concrete test prediction, name a materially distinct alternative consistent with every pair, and identify a specific observation in a new pair that would distinguish them and alter the test prediction. # Demo analysis and budget discipline

## Analyze each pair before the next action

For every returned demonstration, write down the exact input/output dimensions, palette, and cell-level mappings. Identify both transformed cells and plausible lookalikes left unchanged. Separate (a) the selector—what region, object, relation, or source cells contribute—from (b) the operation/encoding—how those selected cells generate the output. Check all candidate rules against the complete pair, not merely the visually obvious changes.

## Request discipline

Before requesting a demo, be able to state:
1. The leading hypothesis and its concrete prediction for the current test.
2. A distinct alternative that also fits all evidence so far.
3. The specific observation in another demo that would separate the two and could change the test answer.

## After incorrect feedback

Binary incorrect feedback rejects the entire candidate, not just its color or one cell. Reassess selector, operation, mapping/alignment, dimensions, and palette independently. Do not submit a superficial variant. Use remaining demos only for a named ambiguity; use remaining submissions for materially distinct, demo-supported hypotheses.

Reproduce every demonstration output exactly, including output shape and unchanged cells. Then apply the validated mapping to the test, validate row count/widths and legal colors, and serialize exactly one action JSON object. For compression-like tasks, establish the source-to-output mapping separately from the color/value encoding; matching dimensions alone is not evidence that the chosen half or projection is right.

# Demonstration analysis checklist

Use this compact worksheet before committing to an ARC transformation.

## Pairwise comparison

- Verify input and output dimensions and enumerate all cells whose colors differ.
- Describe the changed-cell set by coordinates, color, and connected components.
- Check whether the demonstrated seed/object is preserved, recolored, or extended.
- Test candidate geometry against the *exact* output: direction, length, symmetry, spacing, endpoints, object/color exclusions, and edge handling.
- Confirm that cells predicted to change do change and that cells predicted to remain unchanged do remain unchanged.

## Applying a rule to a new grid

- Identify the same kind of seed using object structure and color, not just incidental background matches.
- Generate predicted edits in a copy of the input; preserve source data for comparison.
- Resolve overlaps and collisions only according to demonstrated behavior. If this remains ambiguous, request another demo.
- Validate row count, each row's width, legal color values, and JSON encoding before submission.

## Decision discipline

A single example can support several different rules. Prefer an additional demonstration when it can distinguish those rules; avoid treating a loose visual resemblance or a broad scan for repeated colors as confirmation.

# Demo checkpoint for complex, multi-object tasks

Use this checkpoint after every received pair, especially when the grid contains many scattered components and the transformation selector is unclear.

1. Compare input and output cell-by-cell and list all edits. Group edits by connected component and source/destination color.
2. Enumerate the relevant same-color components, including unchanged ones. For each, record its normalized occupied-cell mask, bounding box, position, and relationship to distinctive objects, lines, or markers. Treat unchanged lookalikes as negative evidence.
3. Separate the *selection rule* (which component is targeted) from the *operation* (recoloring, copying, completion, or movement). Check candidate rules against every edited and unedited component in every demo.
4. Make an explicit test-grid prediction under the leading rule. Before requesting another demo, state the unresolved alternative and how its possible outcomes would distinguish the rule. If no specific ambiguity remains, submit; do not use all available demos by default.
5. Treat the demo cap as a maximum, not a quota. Repeated requests without incorporating evidence incur cost while adding no reasoning value.

For large grids, use a component inventory and exact masks rather than intuitive visual resemblance. Normalize masks by subtracting each object's top-left coordinate so shape comparisons survive different positions, dimensions, and palettes. Verify every demo's complete diff, including unchanged plausible matches, before applying the rule to the test.

# Classify demo outputs before requesting another pair

A returned demonstration should change the solver's model before another request is made. Parse the input's marker colors and coordinates, then inspect the output globally—not only around the original markers. Classify the output as (a) a uniform-color fill, (b) periodic/cyclic color tiling, (c) a geometric completion, or (d) another transformation. For tilings, infer the ordered color cycle and both row/column phase from the demo; for uniform fills, check whether all output cells truly share a color. Compare this classification against every available demo, including apparent outliers, and derive the exact test prediction.

Request again only if a specific alternative hypothesis remains consistent with all evidence and another demo could discriminate it. Demo caps are ceilings, not targets: every request has a score cost. Avoid reflexive consecutive requests and do not treat a dramatically different input/output pair as noise; it may reveal the dominant rule or invalidate a prior hypothesis.

# Demo-request checkpoint after each pair

After a demo arrives, do not immediately request another. First compare its input and output exactly and list each changed coordinate with old and new colors; note salient candidates and regions that did not change. Then state internally:

1. The leading rule, including target-selection criteria and transformation separately.
2. Its concrete output prediction for the current test grid.
3. At least one materially distinct plausible alternative and its test prediction.
4. The specific observation in a further demo that would distinguish the alternatives.
5. Why that distinction could change the answer enough to justify the one-point request cost.

Request only when the final two checks are satisfied. If no concrete discriminator is identifiable, or the existing evidence already supports a test prediction, submit the best-supported answer instead of spending another request. In action-only evaluations, keep all analysis internal and output only the required JSON action. This checkpoint prevents consecutive paid requests made before incorporating returned evidence.

# Evidence checkpoint after each demonstration

Every returned demo pair is a decision point, not an automatic cue to request the next pair. Before another request, compare input and output explicitly: list changed coordinates and colors, note near-matching structures that stayed unchanged, and separate the transformation from the rule that selects targets.

Then test the evidence against the current test input. Write down the leading rule and its exact predicted edits, one materially different rule that still fits every pair, and a concrete feature of a prospective demo that would distinguish them and could change the test answer. If that alternative or distinguishing observation cannot be stated, another request is not evidence-led: submit the best-supported prediction rather than spending a demo token by default. In action-only ARC streams, keep all analysis internal and respond with exactly one action JSON. Do not issue consecutive `request_demos` actions without first performing the checkpoint on the newly returned pair.

# Demo request checkpoint

After each received demonstration pair, analyze it before spending another request. Record what the new example adds to the rule and verify the current leading hypothesis against the entire available set. # Directional fills against boundary rails

Use this check when an ARC demo combines a long stripe/edge of one color with scattered single-cell markers of another color.

## Worked evidence pattern

In the observed pair, the long color-9 rails formed an upper-left L and a lower-right L. Isolated color-5 cells near the upper vertical rail were changed to color 4, and color 5 filled horizontally from those seed locations toward the right, stopping at the next isolated color-5 seed or at the far edge. Symmetrically, rows containing color-5 seeds near the right vertical rail were filled leftward to the left edge. Rows/columns without a seed were not filled merely because they lay inside a broad half-plane. Separately, regions adjacent to the horizontal rail segments were filled with color 5 in some fully bounded strips, while gaps remained untouched.

This supports two structural operations rather than one indiscriminate flood: directed marker-to-barrier/edge rays, plus fills of demonstrably enclosed rail-bounded bands. Preserve markers that are not selected as ray origins and do not infer a universal fill of every region inside the L shape from one example.

## Diagnostic checklist

1. List every changed cell coordinate and old/new color. Group changes by row and column.
2. Mark long rails, endpoints, and isolated markers. For each marker, test rays in both directions and identify the nearest stopping boundary or marker.
3. Check no-seed rows/columns as negative evidence; do not extrapolate the line fill into them.
4. Independently map enclosed strips/compartments created by rails. A single demo may show a second fill rule, distinct from marker-directed rays.
5. On test, identify the same rail orientation and marker role. Apply only operations directly supported by the demo; if competing interpretations change a large part of the output, request a further demo rather than guessing.

1. Compare demo input/output cellwise and record every changed coordinate and color.

# Explicit evidence gate for requesting demos

2. State the leading hypothesis and its concrete prediction for the current test.
3. Name a materially distinct alternative that also explains all received demos.
